name: Saudi Arabia
region: Nationwide — Riyadh, Jeddah, Eastern Province, Asir
summary: 13 million migrant workers (42% of Saudi Arabia's total population) are subject to the kafala sponsorship system. Saudi Arabia recorded record-high executions for a second consecutive year. Women have been sentenced to decades in prison for social media posts. Saudi border guards killed hundreds of Ethiopian migrants at the Yemen border. Sportswashing events proceed as human rights deteriorate.
context:
Saudi Arabia presents a paradox visible to anyone paying attention: massive international sports events, cultural openings, and 'Vision 2030' modernization announcements coexist with systematic human rights violations that are worsening by virtually every measure.

The kafala (sponsorship) system subjects 13 million migrant workers — 42% of Saudi Arabia's total population — to a system that ties their legal status to their employer, making them vulnerable to exploitation, wage theft, passport confiscation, and effective imprisonment in the country if they try to leave without employer permission. Migrant workers, primarily from South Asia, Southeast Asia, and Africa, build Saudi Arabia's infrastructure and run its households in conditions that human rights organizations consistently document as forced labor.

Saudi Arabia's execution rate hit record highs in 2022, 2023, and continues elevated. Many executions follow trials that do not meet minimum international standards — including confessions extracted under torture and capital charges applied to offenses that should carry no such penalty. Drug possession accounts for a significant portion of executions.

Women's rights activists who advocated for the right to drive — the same right the government eventually granted in 2018 — received extraordinary sentences: Salma al-Shehab received 34 years in prison, Nourah al-Qahtani 45 years, for tweets and social media posts. Those imprisoned have been subjected to documented torture, including sexual violence.

Saudi border guards killing Ethiopian migrants attempting to cross from Yemen constitutes a documented pattern of extrajudicial killings at the southern border. Saudi Arabia's multibillion-dollar investments in golf (LIV), football (Premier League), Formula 1, boxing, and entertainment are explicitly described by Saudi officials as image management — 'sportswashing' in human rights organizations' terminology.

awareness: Share the kafala system reality: 13 million people in Saudi Arabia live in a system that ties their legal status to their employer — this is structural forced labor
Highlight the sentences: 34 and 45 years in prison for tweets. This is happening in the country hosting major international sporting events
Amplify the voices of Saudi women's rights activists in exile, including those who have been separated from their children as a form of pressure
Raise awareness about migrant deaths at the Saudi-Yemen border — Ethiopian migrants killed by border guards as they attempted to cross
Challenge sports fans and media to engage with the human rights context of Saudi-hosted or Saudi-funded sporting events
political: Urge your government to raise kafala reform as a condition of trade and investment agreements with Saudi Arabia — 13 million people deserve labor rights
Demand immediate and unconditional release of women's rights activists imprisoned for peaceful advocacy, including those with extraordinarily long sentences
Push for an independent UN investigation into killings of Ethiopian migrants at Saudi Arabia's border with Yemen
Advocate for meaningful reform of the kafala system, not just cosmetic changes that leave structural vulnerabilities in place
Support calls for sports governing bodies to develop and enforce human rights standards for tournament hosting — silence is complicity in sportswashing
